entries.ipa: /ɔlˈðoʊ/ (also /ɑlˈðoʊ/ for speakers with the cot–caught merger)
entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Although [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], although [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the although clause when it comes first. When it follows, put a comma before although — the concession is supplementary, unlike a trailing because clause, which takes no comma. Drop it only when the two clauses are short and tightly fused.
variants: altho
tho' (informal or poetic writing only; not standard prose)
entries.meaning: Introduces a fact that makes the main clause surprising. Unlike but, it subordinates — the although clause is the concession and the main clause carries the point, so which clause you put it on changes what the sentence is arguing. Against though it is the heavier, more written of the two, and it can never be tacked onto the end of a sentence as an afterthought.
examples: Although the store closed at nine, they let us finish shopping.
She took the job, although the pay was worse than what she had been making.
Although it rained all weekend, the festival went ahead.
He never mentioned the diagnosis, although he must have known for months.
Although I understand the decision, I don't agree with it.
The recipe works with frozen berries, although fresh ones give you better color.

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also a preposition (works as a paralegal), half of the comparative correlative as … as, a relative pronoun after such and the same (such delays as we saw), and a causal and a temporal subordinator
entries.register: neutral to literary in this concessive use
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (with inversion)
entries.pattern: [adjective/adverb/bare verb] as [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · As [adjective] as [subject] [verb], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted as clause. This construction is essentially always fronted; it does not trail comfortably.
variants: as … as (the doubled form, more common in American speech: as tired as I was)
entries.meaning: Concessive as takes the word being conceded and throws it in front of the conjunction — try as he might, tired as I was, strange as it sounds. That inversion is the only signal, which is why this as has to be kept apart from causal as (As it was raining, we drove) and temporal as (She called as I was leaving): same word, same spelling, different word order. And the conjunction is only part of the word's day job — as is also a preposition (She works as a paralegal), the second half of the comparative as … as (as cold as it looks), and a relative pronoun after such and the same (such problems as we found). Nothing but position tells them apart.
examples: Try as he might, he could not get the lawn mower to start.
Tired as I was, I stayed up to watch the returns.
Strange as it sounds, the cheaper model outlasted the expensive one.
Cold as it was, the kids refused to come inside.
Search as they did, the divers never found the wreck.
Hard as the team fought, they were down twenty at the half.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.register: neutral to formal (a staple of journalism)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession with simultaneity
entries.pattern: Even as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] even as [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. A comma before a trailing even as clause is optional and usually left out, since the two events are being presented as one moment.
entries.meaning: Marks two things happening at the same time that ought not to go together — a contrast in the calendar rather than in the logic. Plain as would give you nothing but simultaneity; even as adds the sting. It is the standard way American reporters frame a contradiction they are not allowed to call one.
examples: Even as the company announced layoffs, it was posting new job listings.
She kept smiling even as the interviewer cut her off for the third time.
Even as the levees held, forecasters warned that the second surge would be worse.
He insisted the deal was dead even as his lawyers were drafting the terms.
Even as ticket prices climbed, attendance hit a record.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Even though [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], even though [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause when it comes first; comma before it when it follows.
entries.meaning: The emphatic although. It insists that the fact in its clause is genuinely known and genuinely true, and that is the whole line between it and even if, where the fact is only supposed: even though it's raining means it is raining, even if it rains leaves the rain open.
examples: Even though we left at five, we still hit traffic on the bridge.
He paid the full invoice, even though half the work was never done.
Even though she's allergic, she keeps two cats.
They kept the store open through the winter, even though it lost money every month.
Even though I've seen it four times, I cried again at the end.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over occasions
entries.pattern: Even when [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] even when [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. No comma when it trails — the clause names a case the main claim has to survive, so it is integrated rather than supplementary.
entries.meaning: The member of the even family that quantifies over occasions instead of a single fact or a single hypothetical. Even though he's tired concedes one thing that is true right now; even if he's tired leaves it open; even when he's tired says the main clause holds on every such occasion, the least likely one included. It is the plain alternative to no matter when and to a whenever clause pushed onto its hardest case.
examples: Even when the store is empty, there's a wait at the register.
She takes the stairs even when she's carrying groceries.
Even when he's flatly wrong, he sounds completely sure of himself.
The heat doesn't kick on even when it drops below freezing.
Even when we book months ahead, we end up in the middle seats.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Much as [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · As much as [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause], much as [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause, which is where it sits in nearly every case. It can trail, and there it keeps the comma, because a concession is supplementary: I'll have to pass, much as I'd like to be there.
variants: as much as (the more common form in American speech)
entries.meaning: A concession about the speaker's own feelings: "I like this a great deal, and the main clause still stands." It almost always attaches to a verb of liking, admiring, wanting, or hating, which makes it the standard polite way to decline. Although I'd like to reports a fact; much as I'd like to reports a fact and a regret.
examples: Much as I admire her, I wouldn't want to work for her.
As much as I love that neighborhood, we can't afford it.
Much as it pains me to say it, the second album is better.
As much as he complains about the commute, he has never once been late.
Much as the committee wanted to fund every proposal, the budget wouldn't stretch.
I'll have to pass on Saturday, much as I'd like to be there.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.register: formal or literary; much as is the ordinary American form
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Much though [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause], much though [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause, which is where it nearly always sits. Comma before it when it trails, because a concession is supplementary. It is a subordinator, not an adverb, so no semicolon question arises.
variants: much as (the standard American form)
as much as
entries.meaning: The bookish twin of much as — the same meaning, the same attachment to verbs of liking, wanting, and admiring, but a register higher and far commoner in British writing than in American. Americans meet it in literary prose and in speeches reaching for a formal note; what actually comes out in speech is much as or as much as.
examples: Much though I admire her scholarship, this chapter does not hold together.
Much though the town wanted the factory, nobody wanted the traffic that came with it.
He declined the nomination, much though it flattered him to be asked.
Much though it pains me to agree with the man, he is right about the drainage.
Much though she loved the house, the commute finally decided it.

entries.type: subordinating (also a conjunctive adverb in final position)
entries.register: neutral; the final-position adverb is informal
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Though [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause], though [subject] [verb]. · [adjective/noun/bare verb] though [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [statement], though. (final adverb)
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted though clause and before a trailing one. As a sentence-final adverb it is always set off by a comma: I like it, though.
entries.meaning: The lighter, more spoken twin of although, and the only member of the family that also works as a stand-alone adverb meaning "however," parked at the end of a sentence. It takes the inverted concessive pattern too (cold though it was), which although cannot.
examples: Though the recipe calls for buttermilk, regular milk works fine.
We took the long way, though nobody was in a hurry.
Cold though it was, we ate out on the patio.
"The car's twelve years old." "It runs, though."
Though she'd never admit it, the surprise party got to her.
It's a small apartment. The light is incredible, though.

entries.type: subordinating, with the older pleonastic complementizer that attached
entries.register: archaic — Early Modern English; you meet it in Shakespeare and in seventeenth-century verse, and in no modern register
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Though that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], though that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause, exactly as with bare though. Modern editions of older texts keep the that and punctuate the clause as though it were not there.
variants: though (the modern form)
if that, when that, for that, because that (the same doubled pattern on other conjunctions)
entries.meaning: Early Modern English let a subordinator take a redundant that as a clause marker — though that, if that, when that, for that — and the doubled form died out over the seventeenth century. Nothing separates though that from though in meaning; the extra word is grammatical scaffolding, and for a poet it was also a spare syllable. Read straight past it.
examples: "Though that his joy be joy, / Yet throw such changes of vexation on't." (Othello, I.i)
"If I do prove her haggard, / Though that her jesses were my dear heart-strings, / I'd whistle her off." (Othello, III.iii)
Though that the night was far spent, the watch kept its post.
Though that he were the king's own son, the law would have him.
The town gave up nothing, though that the siege ran on through the winter.

entries.type: subordinating — a frozen instance of the inverted concessive as
entries.register: neutral to literary; fully current in American writing, a little bookish in speech
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, with the verb thrown in front of the conjunction
entries.pattern: Try as [subject] might, [main clause]. · Try as [subject] would/will/did, [main clause]. · Try as [subject] might to [verb], [main clause]. · [bare verb] as [subject] might, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause. The construction is fronted in nearly every case; trailing it (he never got it started, try as he might) is possible, and there the comma is required, since it lands as an afterthought.
variants: try as I might, try as he might, try as they might (the pronoun tracks the subject)
try as one will
search as they did, push as he would (the same frame on other verbs)
entries.meaning: The most frozen instance of concessive as: a bare verb is thrown in front of the conjunction and the modal is left standing behind it, giving "no matter how hard the subject tried." The verb is not limited to try — search as they did, push as he would — but try as one might is the shape Americans actually reach for, and the main clause behind it is almost always a failure.
examples: Try as he might, he could not get the pilot light to stay lit.
Try as I might, I cannot make the deposits match the register.
Try as they might, the auditors never found where the money went.
Try as she might to sound neutral, her opinion came through in every paragraph.
The stain came back every spring, try as we might to seal the ceiling.
Search as they did, the divers never located the second engine.

entries.ipa: /wɛn/ (also /hwɛn/ for speakers who keep the wh-) · unstressed /wən/
entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also the ordinary temporal subordinator, an interrogative adverb (When did you get in?), a relative adverb (the year when we moved), a complementizer in noun clauses (I don't know when it ships), and a noun (the when and the where)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (an extension of the clause of time)
entries.pattern: [main clause] when [clause]. · When [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Normally no comma before a trailing concessive when clause — it is integrated, not supplementary. Comma after it if you front it.
entries.meaning: The same word that marks time also marks concession, and only sense tells them apart: Why buy it when you can borrow it? is not about a moment, it is about a contradiction. Concessive when almost always follows the main clause and usually carries a note of complaint or challenge that although does not.
examples: Why pay for parking when the lot two blocks over is free?
He asked for a raise when he'd been there six weeks.
She apologized when the whole thing was my fault.
When you already own the tools, hiring somebody makes no sense.
They cut the arts budget when enrollment in those classes was going up.

entries.type: subordinating; also a noun (stay a while, worth your while) and a verb (while away an afternoon)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession or contrast (also of time)
entries.pattern: While [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], while [clause].
entries.punctuation: The comma is what separates the two meanings. Contrastive while takes one — He's methodical, while his partner works on instinct — and temporal while does not: She read while I cooked. Fronted, it always takes a comma after the clause.
entries.meaning: While does three jobs as a conjunction — time, contrast, and concession — and American readers sort them by position and comma. Concessive while ("although") is normal at the front of a sentence; contrastive while ("whereas") is normal in the middle with a comma in front of it. If a sentence could be read either as time or as contrast, rewrite it. Outside the conjunction the same spelling is a noun (it took a while, worth your while) and a verb (we whiled away the afternoon), which is why awhile and a while trip people up: the one-word adverb modifies a verb, the two-word noun phrase follows a preposition.
examples: While I agree with the goal, I think the timeline is fantasy.
He's methodical, while his partner works on instinct.
While the paint is technically dry, I wouldn't lean on it.
Our office got new chairs, while the warehouse crew got nothing.
While nobody disputes the numbers, everybody disputes what they mean.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.register: British; dated or affected in American English
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession or contrast (also of time)
entries.pattern: Whilst [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], whilst [clause].
entries.punctuation: Same as while: comma after a fronted clause, comma before a trailing contrastive one.
variants: while (the standard American form)
entries.meaning: The British counterpart of while, in every one of its senses. Americans read it as affected or as a signal that the writer is British, and it turns up in American prose almost only when someone is reaching for formality. Use while. Its cousins amongst, amidst, and learnt carry the same flag.
examples: Whilst the committee acknowledged the delay, it declined to apologize.
She studied in Leeds, whilst her brother stayed in Cork.
Whilst I take your point, the deadline has not moved.
The tenants were told to vacate whilst repairs were carried out.
Whilst rare, such errors are not unheard of.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb by function — a Latin preposition in form, taking a noun phrase or a citation and never a clause
entries.register: formal — American legal citation and academic prose; it exists nowhere else
entries.clause: none — it points at an authority or a writer holding the opposite view
entries.pattern: [statement]. Contra, [citation]. · Contra [name], [main clause]. · [main clause] (contra [name]).
entries.punctuation: In a citation sentence, a comma after it and then the authority: Contra, Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938). Before a name in running prose it takes no comma of its own — contra Quine — and the whole phrase is fenced with commas or parentheses when it interrupts. It is not a conjunction and cannot join two independent clauses.
variants: but see, but cf. (the English citation signals that do the same job)
pace (which bows before it disagrees)
contra proferentem, contra bonos mores (fixed legal phrases — a different word class)
entries.meaning: Latin "against," and in American usage a pointer rather than a connector: it flags an authority or a writer holding the opposite of what the sentence just said. Citation manuals keep it as the signal for directly contrary authority, and scholarship borrows it to name the person being argued with. Contra Smith means "Smith says otherwise"; pace Smith means "Smith says otherwise, and I mean no disrespect."
examples: Contra, Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938).
Every circuit to reach the question has read the clause narrowly. Contra, a single unpublished order from 1974.
Contra Quine, the analytic–synthetic distinction survives in a weakened form.
Most editors treat the manuscript as a scribal copy (contra Hollander, who calls it an autograph).
The brief cites four cases for the proposition and, contra, none against it.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb by function — a two-word preposition, taking a noun phrase or a fused relative what clause and never a bare finite clause
entries.clause: none of its own — a fronted adverbial that sets the main clause against a belief, an expectation, or a rule
entries.pattern: Contrary to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Contrary to what [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], contrary to [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, and that comma is not optional — the phrase is a full adverbial. It cannot join two independent clauses: The trail is open, contrary to what you heard, it closes in November is a comma splice.
variants: contrary to popular belief, contrary to expectation (fixed collocations)
contrary to the fact that (wordy — cut it)
contra (the Latin citation form)
entries.meaning: Sets the main clause against something someone believes, expects, or has ordered. Its everyday use is corrective — contrary to what you've heard — and its legal use is stricter, where a thing done contrary to a rule was done in violation of it. It needs a noun phrase, so to hang it on a clause you have to insert what (contrary to what the sign says) or the fact that.
examples: Contrary to popular belief, the bridge is older than the highway.
Contrary to what the listing said, the unit has no washer-dryer hookup.
She kept the receipts, contrary to the office's usual practice.
Contrary to the doctor's advice, he flew home the next morning.
Contrary to every forecast we saw, the storm turned east at the last minute.
The permit was issued contrary to the zoning ordinance and was later revoked.

entries.type: subordinating; except on its own is a preposition (everyone except me) and, in frozen phrases, a verb (present company excepted)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of exception and contrast
entries.pattern: [main clause], except that [clause]. · [main clause]. Except that [clause]. · [main clause], except [when/where/if] [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before a trailing except that clause — it withdraws part of what was just claimed, so it is supplementary, never integrated. It essentially never fronts ahead of its own main clause: Except that the fan rattled, the room was quiet is not idiomatic. When the exception needs weight of its own, give it a period or a dash and let it stand as a fragment.
variants: except
except for the fact that (wordy — cut it)
only (the spoken equivalent: I'd have called, only I lost your number)
entries.meaning: Subtracts a piece of the main clause instead of conceding a point against it, and that is what keeps it out of the although family: although the room was quiet grants a fact and moves on, while except that the fan rattled takes something back. American speech does the same work with bare but or only; except that is what writing reaches for when the exception has to be named precisely.
examples: The apartment would be perfect, except that there's no parking on the block.
Nothing about the trip went wrong, except that the rental car smelled like smoke.
I'd have finished the draft, except that the power went out at nine.
The two engines are identical, except that the newer one carries a longer warranty.
She remembers the whole evening. Except that she can't say who drove her home.
The branch is open every day, except when the holiday falls on a Monday.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈflɪp ˌsaɪd/ · casually /ɑn ə ˈflɪp saɪd/
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal)
entries.register: informal — spoken American English; too casual for a brief, a contract, or a formal report
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial linking two independent clauses
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. On the flip side, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; on the flip side, [independent clause]. · On the flip side of [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it. Because it is an adverb and not a conjunction, a comma alone in front of it between two independent clauses is a comma splice — use a period or a semicolon: The rent is cheap; on the flip side, the commute is an hour.
variants: on the other hand (the neutral form)
then again
flip side, the flip side is (that) (the same image as a noun)
entries.meaning: The casual American cousin of on the other hand, borrowed from the B-side of a 45. It introduces the offsetting half of a trade-off, and it works best when the two halves really are two faces of one thing — cheap rent and a long commute — rather than two unrelated facts. In anything more formal than an email, write on the other hand.
examples: The job pays well. On the flip side, you're on call every other weekend.
We got the house under asking; on the flip side, the roof is going this year.
On the flip side, nobody in Tucson has ever had to shovel a driveway.
Streaming gutted album sales. On the flip side, a nobody in Ohio can reach ten thousand listeners overnight.
She's the fastest coder on the team; on the flip side, nobody else can read what she writes.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb by function — a Latin ablative used as a preposition, taking a name or a noun phrase and never a clause
entries.register: formal, academic — criticism, philosophy, and the more literary reviews; a scholar's word, and unknown outside that world
entries.clause: none — a parenthetical adverbial naming the authority being contradicted
entries.pattern: Pace [name], [main clause]. · [main clause], pace [name]. · [main clause] (pace [name]).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase; commas or parentheses on both sides when it interrupts. No comma between pace and the name it governs. It cannot join two independent clauses.
variants: with all due respect to, with apologies to (the plain-English forms)
contra (blunter, and without the courtesy)
entries.meaning: Latin for "by the leave of," and it means "with apologies to X, who thinks otherwise." It concedes that a respected authority holds the opposite view and then proceeds anyway, which makes it the politest adversative in academic English — and the most easily misread, since it looks like the ordinary English word and is said PAY-see. Against contra, which simply files an opposing citation, pace bows first.
examples: Pace Dr. Johnson, the poem is not a failure.
The tax, pace its defenders, falls hardest on the people it was written to help.
Pace the committee's report, enrollment has been flat for a decade.
Chaucer was not writing for a courtly audience here, pace Robertson.
Pace my colleagues in the department, the second edition is the better text.

entries.type: subordinating; save is far commoner as a preposition (all save one) and as an ordinary verb
entries.register: formal and literary, verging on archaic — not neutral, and out of place in ordinary American prose
entries.clause: adverbial clause of exception and contrast
entries.pattern: [main clause], save that [clause]. · [main clause], save [noun phrase]. (preposition) · [main clause], save for [noun phrase]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Comma before the save that clause, exactly as with except that. It does not front.
variants: save
save for
saving that (archaic)
except that (the neutral everyday form)
entries.meaning: The formal twin of except that, and the register gap between them is wide: save that belongs to literary narration, appellate opinions, and deliberate period voice, and in a memo or an email it reads as a costume. Use except that. What is still alive in American English is the preposition save or save for — the lot was empty save for one truck — and even that sits a notch above neutral.
examples: The record is complete, save that two pages are missing from the appendix.
Nothing in the house had changed, save that someone had moved the piano.
The statute reaches every carrier, save that municipal fleets are exempt.
He remembered nothing of the crossing, save that it had been bitterly cold.
The street was dark, save for a light in the second-floor window. (preposition, not a conjunction)

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also the ordinary locative subordinator (Put it where it belongs), an interrogative adverb (Where is it?), a relative adverb (the town where she grew up), and a noun (the where and the when)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of contrast (also of place)
entries.pattern: Where [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], where [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause and before the trailing one. That comma is also what tells a reader you mean contrast and not place.
entries.meaning: Contrastive where sets one case against another — "in this version X, in that one Y." It is the reviewer's and the analyst's conjunction. Where whereas balances two whole propositions, contrastive where usually balances two versions of the same thing.
examples: Where his first novel was tight and mean, this one sprawls.
The old system logged every request, where the new one samples.
Where other teams rebuild, this one just keeps signing veterans.
She writes in long paragraphs, where he can't get past two sentences.
Where the state requires a permit, the county only asks for a notice.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of contrast
entries.pattern: [main clause], whereas [clause]. · Whereas [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Always a comma before a trailing whereas clause — it is supplementary, never integrated. Comma after it when fronted. In legal preambles (Whereas the parties agree …) the older sense "given that" survives, and each whereas clause is closed with a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Pure contrast, no concession: it says the two clauses differ, not that one defeats the other. That is the line against although — Although I like coffee, I drink tea implies a tension, while I drink coffee, whereas she drinks tea implies only a difference. While does the same job in a lower register.
examples: My brother loves horror movies, whereas I can't get through the trailers.
Whereas the coastal counties voted one way, the interior went the other.
Diesel engines gain efficiency under load, whereas gas engines lose it.
She was hired for her research, whereas he was hired to run the lab.
Whereas the first draft ran ninety pages, the final version is thirty.

entries.type: subordinating inside the fixed frame assuming arguendo that; the bare word is a Latin adverb ("in the course of argument") and connects nothing by itself
entries.register: formal, legal — American briefs and judicial opinions, and essentially nowhere else
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: Assuming arguendo that [clause], [main clause]. · Assuming, arguendo, that [clause], [main clause]. · Even assuming arguendo [clause], [main clause]. · [verb phrase] arguendo.
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. The adverb itself is often fenced with commas inside the frame — assuming, arguendo, that the statute applies — and either punctuation is standard.
variants: assuming arguendo
for the sake of argument, assuming for the sake of argument that (the plain-English forms)
conceding the point arguendo
entries.meaning: A lawyer's even if. It grants a premise the writer does not accept, purely to show that the argument fails even on the opponent's own terms, and the Latin is there so that nobody can later quote the concession as an admission. In a brief it is standard and expected; anywhere else, write even if or for the sake of argument.
examples: Assuming arguendo that the search was lawful, the evidence was still gathered outside the scope of the warrant.
Even assuming arguendo the plaintiff has standing, the claim is time-barred.
The court accepted, arguendo, that the notice was defective, and affirmed on other grounds.
Assuming, arguendo, that a contract was formed, no party ever performed under it.
Counsel conceded the point arguendo and moved on to the damages calculation.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: Even if [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] even if [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause when it comes first; normally no comma when it follows, because the condition is part of what the main clause is claiming.
entries.meaning: Grants a condition that has not happened, then says the main clause holds anyway. That is the whole difference from even though, which grants a fact. It often pairs with would or still, and with a past-perfect verb it turns counterfactual: even if you had told me.
examples: Even if the flight is on time, I won't get in before midnight.
I'm going even if nobody else does.
Even if you had told me, I'm not sure I could have stopped it.
The policy wouldn't have covered the damage even if she had filed the day it happened.
Even if the numbers hold up, the conclusion still doesn't follow.

entries.type: subordinating; the same word heads conditional clauses (If it rains, we'll move inside) and noun clauses after verbs of asking and knowing (Ask if they're open)
entries.register: formal or literary in this concessive use; conditional if is neutral
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, usually reduced to a phrase
entries.pattern: [statement], if [adjective]. · [determiner] [adjective], if [adjective], [noun]. · If [adjective/noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides when concessive if interrupts — a clever, if flawed, argument. A fronted reduced clause takes a comma after it. Never leave it uncommaed, or a reader will take it for the conditional.
entries.meaning: A compressed although, almost always attached to an adjective rather than to a full clause, and almost always in writing. It concedes one quality while asserting another: a useful, if expensive, tool. Conditional if asks whether something is true; concessive if takes for granted that it is and grants it anyway.
examples: The plan is bold, if risky.
If poor, he was never once late with the rent.
It was a clear, if unwelcome, answer.
She gave a short, if pointed, reply to the board.
The remodel produced a functional, if charmless, kitchen.
If not elegant, the solution at least worked.

entries.type: subordinating; bare regardless is a conjunctive adverb (Regardless, the flight left on time) and regardless of is a preposition (regardless of cost) — neither can take a clause until whether or the fact that is bolted on
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: Regardless of whether [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] regardless of whether [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails.
variants: irrespective of whether (more formal). Irregardless is nonstandard in every register — do not use it in writing.
entries.meaning: Says the main clause holds across both branches of an open question. It is the contractual version of whether or not: same meaning, four more syllables, and a home in policies, statutes, and memos rather than in speech.
examples: Regardless of whether the grant comes through, the study starts in March.
Tenants must be given sixty days' notice regardless of whether the sale closes.
Regardless of whether you attend, please submit your comments in writing.
The application fee is nonrefundable regardless of whether the applicant is admitted.
Regardless of whether the recall is expanded, the plant stays closed through August.

entries.type: subordinating, and correlative in the split form whether … or (not); the same whether also heads noun clauses (I asked whether it was open)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: Whether or not [clause], [main clause]. · Whether [clause] or not, [main clause]. · Whether [clause A] or [clause B], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the whole fronted clause, and no comma between the whether half and the or half. No comma when the clause trails.
variants: whether … or
whether … or not
entries.meaning: Runs through every alternative and says the outcome is the same in all of them. Keep it apart from noun-clause whether: I don't know whether she's coming is an object, takes no comma, and cannot lose the or not, while concessive whether or not you agree is an adverbial and always can.
examples: Whether or not you agree, the vote stands.
The bill comes on the first whether you use the service or not.
Whether the forecast is right or the storm turns, we're canceling the trip.
She's going to say what she thinks whether or not the cameras are on.
Whether or not it was intentional, the effect was the same.

entries.type: subordinating (a different word from the conjunctive adverb however)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal — "no matter how"
entries.pattern: However [adjective/adverb] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · However [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · However many/much [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] however [adjective/adverb] [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the whole however clause and no comma after however itself. That is the test that separates the two words: However, he tried is the adverb; However hard he tried, is the subordinator. The adverb also needs a semicolon or a period before it when it stands between two independent clauses; the subordinator never does.
variants: howsoever (archaic or legal)
entries.meaning: Means "no matter how," and it grabs the adjective or adverb it scopes over: however hard, however carefully, however many. Learners meet the conjunctive adverb however ("but") first and then misread this one; the giveaway is that the subordinator is never followed by a comma and always has a clause hanging off it.
examples: However hard he tried, he could not get the door back on its hinges.
However you slice the numbers, the program loses money.
She answers every email however long it takes.
However many times I explain it, somebody asks again.
However carefully you pack them, a few glasses always break.

entries.type: subordinating, and also a conjunctive adverb meaning "however" — it inherits both jobs from however
entries.register: dialectal and archaic — nineteenth-century American rural speech and the local-color fiction that reproduced it, and still heard from older Appalachian and Ozark speakers. It is not standard in any written register.
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal — "no matter how"; also a sentence adverbial
entries.pattern: Howsomever [adjective/adverb] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · Howsomever [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [statement]; howsomever, [statement]. (adverb)
entries.punctuation: As a subordinator, a comma after the whole clause and no comma after howsomever itself — the same test that separates the two howevers. As an adverb it needs a period or a semicolon in front of it between two independent clauses, and a comma after.
variants: however (the standard form)
howsoever (the formal and legal form)
howsumever, howsever, howsomdever (other dialect spellings)
entries.meaning: A folk extension of howsoever, and the extra syllable is exactly what marks it: howsoever turns up in a deed, howsomever turns up in a character's mouth. Americans meet it in dialect writing — Twain and the local-color novelists — and in the speech of older rural speakers, and dropping it into ordinary prose reads as either a mistake or a costume.
examples: "Howsomever, I done it, and I warn't sorry for it afterwards, neither."
Howsomever you figure it, that fence is on our side of the line.
He never learned to read; howsomever, he could price a load of timber in his head.
Howsomever hard the winter came on, the stock got fed first.
"It ain't much of a road, howsomever it'll carry you to the river."

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over degree
entries.pattern: No matter how [adjective/adverb] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · No matter how many/much [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] no matter how [adjective/adverb] [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. When it trails, a comma before it is optional — include it if the clause lands as an afterthought.
entries.meaning: The plain-English twin of subordinating however, and by far the more common of the two in American speech. It scopes over a degree — how hard, how long, how many — and says the main clause survives all of them.
examples: No matter how hard I try, I can't parallel park.
The stain comes back no matter how many times we scrub it.
No matter how early we leave, we hit the same traffic.
He won't sell, no matter how much they offer.
No matter how carefully you read the contract, something is buried in there.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: [main clause] — no matter that [clause]. · No matter that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Usually set off with a dash, a comma, or a sentence of its own, because it arrives as an afterthought rather than as a condition. Comma after it when fronted.
entries.meaning: The one member of the no matter family that takes a plain statement instead of a question word, and it means "although," not "regardless of which." It comes with a dismissive shrug built in: the conceded fact is being brushed aside, not weighed.
examples: He was introduced as the founder — no matter that he joined in year four.
No matter that the lease says otherwise, they've been parking there for years.
The story ran as fact, no matter that two sources had already retracted.
She was blamed for the delay, no matter that she had flagged the problem in April.
No matter that it was pouring, the coach kept them on the field.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over things and outcomes
entries.pattern: No matter what [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · No matter what [verb phrase], [main clause]. · No matter what [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] no matter what [subject] [verb]. · [main clause], no matter what. (fixed tag, nothing following)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; comma before the bare tag no matter what at the end of a sentence.
variants: no matter which (when the choice comes from a known set — it has its own entry below)
entries.meaning: Ranges over every possible thing or outcome. Unlike whatever, it can only be adverbial — you cannot make it the subject or object of anything — which is why No matter what you decide, I'm with you works and No matter what you decide is fine does not.
examples: No matter what the inspector finds, we're closing on Friday.
I'll be at the airport, no matter what.
No matter what I cook, he asks whether there's pizza.
She was going to defend him no matter what the tape showed.
No matter what you've heard, the trail is open all winter.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over time
entries.pattern: No matter when [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] no matter when [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails.
entries.meaning: Says the timing makes no difference. It competes with whenever, which is far more common in the plain time sense; a writer reaches for no matter when when the concession is the point and the schedule is not.
examples: No matter when you call, somebody will pick up.
The bakery has a line out the door no matter when we go.
No matter when the funding clears, construction can't start before spring.
He shows up at the same table no matter when his shift ends.
No matter when they schedule it, half the department will be traveling.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over place
entries.pattern: No matter where [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] no matter where [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails.
entries.meaning: Says the place makes no difference. Against wherever, which can also simply name a place (Put it wherever you like), no matter where is only ever a concession.
examples: No matter where you sit, you can hear the kitchen.
The dog finds the one sunny spot no matter where we move the couch.
No matter where the company relocates, she says she isn't moving.
Cell service drops out no matter where you stand in that building.
No matter where we've lived, the first thing we look for is a decent diner.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over a closed set
entries.pattern: No matter which [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · No matter which [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] no matter which [noun] [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails.
variants: no matter what (when the field is wide open rather than a known set)
entries.meaning: No matter what ranges over everything; no matter which ranges over a list the speaker and the listener already have in front of them — two candidates, three routes, four plans. It stands to whichever exactly as no matter what stands to whatever: same meaning, but adverbial only, so it can never be the subject or object of the main verb.
examples: No matter which route you take, you'll sit in traffic on the bridge.
The premium goes up no matter which plan we pick.
No matter which of the two finalists they hire, somebody on the committee is going to be unhappy.
She'll be up all night no matter which night they schedule it.
No matter which way you read that clause, it doesn't cover this.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over persons
entries.pattern: No matter who [verb phrase], [main clause]. · No matter who [subject] [verb], [main clause]. (when who is the object inside its own clause) · [main clause] no matter who [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails.
variants: no matter whom (formal, and only when the pronoun is an object: no matter whom they appoint)
entries.meaning: Ranges over every person. Like the rest of the family it is adverbial only, and that is the split from whoever: Whoever wins gets the trophy has whoever doing subject duty, while No matter who wins, the trophy stays here bolts a concession onto a sentence that was already complete.
examples: No matter who wins in November, the deficit is still there in January.
She gives the same answer no matter who asks.
No matter who signed off on it, the design is wrong.
The rule applies no matter who you know.
No matter who they hire, that job is going to eat somebody alive.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over reasons
entries.pattern: No matter why [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] no matter why [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails.
variants: whatever the reason (the commoner everyday phrasing)
for whatever reason (a noun-phrase adverbial, not a clause)
entries.meaning: Says the reason makes no difference. It is the thinnest-used member of the family, for two reasons: English already has two shorter ways to say it — whatever the reason, for whatever reason — and why has no live -ever form in American English, so no matter why has no whyever pushing against it the way whenever pushes against no matter when. Reach for it when the sentence is refusing to litigate motive.
examples: No matter why he left, the position is open now.
The late fee applies no matter why the payment missed the due date.
No matter why the numbers moved, the board is going to want an explanation.
They'll suspend your license no matter why you skipped the hearing.
No matter why you're calling, you'll be on hold for twenty minutes.

entries.ipa: /wʌtˈɛvər/ (also /wɑtˈɛvər/, and /hwʌtˈɛvər/ for speakers who keep the wh-) · casually /wəˈɾɛvər/, with the t flapped
entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also a determiner (whatever excuse she gave), a fused relative pronoun heading noun clauses (whatever falls on the floor), and — informally — a one-word dismissive interjection (Whatever.)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal — also heads noun clauses
entries.pattern: Whatever [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · Whatever [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] whatever [subject] [verb]. · [verb] whatever [subject] [verb] (noun clause — no comma)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause when it is a concession at the front of a sentence. No comma when the whatever clause is the subject or object of the main verb — that is a noun clause, not an adverbial. Whatever you decide is fine takes no comma; Whatever you decide, I'll back you does.
variants: whatsoever (dead as a subordinator; alive only as an emphatic tag after a negative: no reason whatsoever)
entries.meaning: Two words in one shape. Concessive whatever means "no matter what" and can be lifted out without breaking the sentence; nominal whatever means "anything that" and cannot. The comma test above is the fastest way to tell them apart.
examples: Whatever you do, don't touch the red switch.
He finds something to complain about whatever we order.
Whatever the reason, the shipment never left the warehouse.
Whatever excuse she gave, the landlord didn't buy it.
Whatever happens tonight, I'm proud of you.
The dog eats whatever falls on the floor. (noun clause — no comma, no concession)

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also the ordinary time subordinator meaning "every time" and a fused relative heading noun clauses (Whenever you get here is fine)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over time — also of time proper
entries.pattern: Whenever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whenever [clause]. · [main clause] whenever. (bare tag, nothing following: Call me whenever) · Whenever [clause] [main-clause verb phrase]. (fused relative heading a noun clause — no comma: Whenever you get here is fine)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. No comma when it trails in the time sense; a comma is fine when the trailing clause is a genuine concession. No comma when the whenever clause is the subject or object of the main verb — that is a noun clause, not an adverbial.
entries.meaning: Mostly a time word meaning "every time," but it turns concessive when the point is that the timing is irrelevant rather than repeated. Whenever you get here is fine is scheduling, Whenever there's a potluck she brings the same casserole is a pattern, and Whenever that photo was taken, it wasn't 1962 is a concession.
examples: Whenever the deal actually closes, the terms won't change.
Call me whenever — I'm up late anyway.
Whenever they schedule the hearing, we'll be ready.
She brings the same casserole whenever there's a potluck.
Whenever that photo was taken, it wasn't 1962.

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also the ordinary place subordinator (Sit wherever you like) and a fused relative heading noun clauses
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over place — also of place proper
entries.pattern: Wherever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] wherever [clause]. · [verb/preposition] wherever [clause]. (fused relative heading a noun clause — no comma) · Wherever [clause] [main-clause verb phrase]. (fused relative as subject — no comma)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted concessive clause; no comma when it trails. No comma when the wherever clause is the subject or object of the main verb — that is a noun clause naming a place, not a concession.
variants: wheresoever (archaic or legal)
entries.meaning: "In any place, and it makes no difference which." The concessive reading is the fronted one; trailing, it usually just names a place, and there the clause is an ordinary adverbial of place rather than a concession.
examples: Wherever they end up, they'll make it work.
He takes that ridiculous pillow wherever he travels.
Wherever the money came from, it wasn't the general fund.
You can pick up the order wherever is closest to you. (fused relative naming a place — no comma, no concession)
Wherever you look in that town, somebody's cousin owns the building.

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also a determiner (whichever route you take) and a fused relative pronoun heading noun clauses (Take whichever you like)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over a known set — also heads noun clauses
entries.pattern: Whichever [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · Whichever [subject] [verb], [main clause]. (as a bare pronoun, no noun following) · [main clause] whichever [noun] [subject] [verb]. · [verb] whichever [noun] [subject] [verb] (noun clause — no comma)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted concessive clause, and a comma before a trailing concessive one, which is supplementary: The winner gets the corner office, whichever of them it turns out to be. No comma when the whichever clause is the subject or object of the main verb — that is a noun clause, not a concession.
variants: whichsoever (archaic or legal)
entries.meaning: Like whatever, except that the alternatives are a closed, known set — two candidates, three routes, four plans. If the speaker has a list in mind, whichever; if the field is wide open, whatever.
examples: Whichever route you take, you'll cross the same bridge.
The winner gets the corner office, whichever of them it turns out to be.
Whichever plan the board picks, somebody's department loses a position.
Whichever way the vote goes, this will be in court by spring.
Take whichever seat you like. (noun clause — no comma)

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also a fused relative pronoun heading noun clauses (Give it to whoever answers)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over persons — also heads noun clauses
entries.pattern: Whoever [verb phrase], [main clause]. · Whoever [subject] [verb], [main clause]. (when whoever is the object inside its own clause) · [main clause] whoever [verb phrase]. · [verb/preposition] whoever [verb phrase] (noun clause — no comma)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted concessive clause; a trailing concessive clause normally goes uncommaed, since it names a case the main claim has to survive. No comma when the clause is the subject or object of the main verb: Whoever left this here owes me a mug.
variants: whomever (formal, and only when the pronoun is the object inside its own clause)
whosoever (archaic or legal)
entries.meaning: "No matter which person." The case trap is real: pick whoever or whomever by the job the word does inside its own clause, not by what comes before it — Give it to whoever answers is correct, because whoever is the subject of answers, not the object of to.
examples: Whoever took the last of the coffee, please start a new pot.
Whoever wins the primary, this district is going to be expensive.
They'll blame the front office whoever they end up hiring.
Whoever they assign to the case, it settles before trial.
Whoever signed for the package, it wasn't anybody in this office.
The prize goes to whoever finishes first. (noun clause — no comma, no concession)

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (participial)
entries.pattern: Admitting that [clause], [main clause]. · Even admitting that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause. It is fronted essentially always; trailing, it reads as a dangling participle.
variants: even admitting that
while admitting that
entries.meaning: Concedes a point for the sake of argument and then rejects the conclusion drawn from it. It belongs to debate and briefs rather than to conversation, and it sits right next to granted that — the difference is that admitting that implies the speaker had been resisting the point up to now.
examples: Admitting that the sample was small, the direction of the result is still striking.
Even admitting that he was provoked, the response was out of all proportion.
Admitting that the deadline slipped, the team delivered more than was asked for.
Admitting that the neighborhood has changed, the zoning argument still doesn't follow.
Even admitting that costs have risen, a forty percent increase is hard to defend.

entries.type: subordinating; bare aside from is a preposition (aside from the rent) and cannot take a clause until the fact that is bolted on
entries.clause: adverbial clause of exception and contrast
entries.pattern: Aside from the fact that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] aside from the fact that [clause]. · Apart from the fact that [clause], [main clause]. · Aside from [noun phrase], [main clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; usually no comma when it trails. Fronting is the normal position, because the exception has to be quarantined before the main clause can make its claim.
variants: apart from the fact that (the same thing, a shade more bookish in American English)
other than the fact that
aside from + noun phrase (a preposition, not a conjunction)
entries.meaning: The exception-flavored member of the the fact that family. Despite the fact that concedes an obstacle and pushes past it; aside from the fact that sets one item off to the side and then rates everything else, which is why it so often carries a dry joke — the thing set aside is usually the thing that matters most. Against except that the split is position and timing: except that trails and takes something back from a claim already made, while aside from the fact that fronts and fences the exception off before the claim arrives.
examples: Aside from the fact that the car has no brakes, it's in great shape.
The proposal is workable aside from the fact that nobody has budgeted for it.
Apart from the fact that she has never managed anyone, she'd be a fine choice.
He had no objection to the paint color aside from the fact that he had picked a different one.
Aside from the fact that it rained all week, the trip was everything we wanted.
Aside from the noise, the apartment is perfect. (preposition, not a conjunction)

entries.type: subordinating (participial)
entries.register: formal — briefs, editorials, and argument generally
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (participial)
entries.pattern: Conceding that [clause], [main clause]. · While conceding that [clause], [main clause]. · Even conceding that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause. It is fronted almost always, and the subject of the main clause has to be the one doing the conceding — otherwise the participle dangles.
variants: while conceding that
even conceding that
granting that
admitting that
entries.meaning: Puts the other side's point on the record and then denies that the point decides anything. Of the three participial concessives it is the most deliberate: admitting that suggests the speaker had been resisting, granting that treats the premise as merely arguable, and conceding that hands over something the speaker would rather have kept.
examples: Conceding that the notice was late, counsel argued that no party had been prejudiced by the delay.
While conceding that enrollment has fallen, the superintendent opposed closing the school.
Even conceding that the first study was flawed, three later ones found the same effect.
Conceding that she had the votes, he still refused to bring the bill to the floor.
Conceding that the repairs were overdue, the landlord denied that the ceiling had ever leaked.

entries.type: subordinating; bare despite is a preposition only (despite the rain) and can never take a clause
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Despite the fact that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] despite the fact that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; usually no comma when it trails.
variants: despite + noun phrase (a preposition, not a conjunction)
entries.meaning: A five-word way of saying although, built only so that the preposition despite can take a clause — which it cannot do on its own. Every American style guide tells you to cut it, and they are right, though the length does make the conceded fact land as an established one.
examples: Despite the fact that the road was closed, three cars were waved through.
The bill passed despite the fact that nobody had read it.
Despite the fact that she had never flown before, she slept the whole way.
They renewed his contract despite the fact that attendance was down a third straight year.
Despite the fact that the warranty had expired, the shop fixed it for free.
related: in spite of the fact that

entries.type: prepositional in form, concessive in force — it takes a noun phrase; for all that is the version that takes a clause
entries.clause: none of its own — a concessive prepositional phrase standing in for a whole clause
entries.pattern: For all [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] for all [noun phrase]. · For all [possessive] [noun], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase. Trailing, it normally goes uncommaed — he never leaves the county for all his talk of traveling — because there it is integrated into the claim rather than supplementary to it.
variants: for all that (the clause-taking form, immediately below)
for all I know, for all I care, for all the good it did (fixed idioms in which for all does take a clause)
despite, in spite of (the neutral prepositions)
entries.meaning: "In spite of," with a shrug in it. What separates it from plain despite is the implication that the thing named should have been enough and wasn't: for all his money says the money ought to have bought something and did not. It attaches most naturally to a possessive noun phrase, and that is the shape American speech keeps alive.
examples: For all his money, he drives a fifteen-year-old pickup.
For all the noise the committee made, nothing in the budget changed.
The alarm system did nothing for all the money we spent on it.
For all her training, the first week on the floor nearly broke her.
For all the talk of a rebuild, they signed two more thirty-year-olds.
He might as well have stayed home, for all the good it did.
related: in spite of the fact that

entries.ipa: /fər ˈɔl ˈðæt/ as the adverb, where that is a stressed demonstrative · /fər ˈɔl ðət/ as the subordinator, where that is an unstressed complementizer
entries.type: subordinating; also a conjunctive adverb meaning "even so," and the bare for all is a preposition (for all his money)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: For all that [clause], [main clause]. · [statement]. For all that, [statement]. (adverb) · For all [noun phrase], [main clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: As a subordinator, comma after the fronted clause. As an adverb meaning "even so," set it off with commas — and use a period or semicolon, never a comma alone, if it stands between two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: Two related jobs. Followed by a clause it means "although": For all that he complains, he never leaves. Standing alone it means "nevertheless": He's rude. For all that, he's the best we have. The related for all plus a noun phrase — for all his money — is a preposition, not a conjunction at all.
examples: For all that he grumbles about the drive, he has never once called out.
The house is drafty and the roof leaks. For all that, we love it.
For all that the reviews were brutal, the show sold out every night.
She was underprepared and, for all that, still the sharpest person in the room.
For all that the technology has changed, the job is the same one my father had.

entries.type: subordinating; bare granted is a conjunctive adverb with its own entry below, and it is also the plain past participle of the verb grant (the permit was granted)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Granted that [clause], [main clause]. · Granting that [clause], [main clause]. · Granted [clause], [main clause]. (with that dropped)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause. Always fronted.
variants: granting that
allowing that
granted with the that dropped
entries.meaning: Concedes a premise in order to attack the inference drawn from it — the arguer's move. Granted that treats the fact as settled, where even if would leave it open. Bare granted, used alone as a reply or a sentence opener, is the same word doing a much more common and much more casual job.
examples: Granted that the numbers are accurate, they still don't support that conclusion.
Granting that she had the authority, the process was not followed.
Granted that the building is historic, it is also unsafe.
Granting that the two cases look alike, the statutes are completely different.
Granted that we were late, the ticket agent didn't have to be rude about it.

entries.term: in spite of the fact that
entries.respell: in SPYTE uv thuh FAKT that
entries.type: subordinating; bare in spite of is a preposition only (in spite of the rain) and can never take a clause; the noun spite inside it is frozen and carries none of its ordinary meaning
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: In spite of the fact that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] in spite of the fact that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; usually no comma when it trails.
variants: in spite of + noun phrase (a preposition, not a conjunction)
entries.meaning: The longest way to say although that is still standard English. It differs from despite the fact that by one word and a shade of tone — in spite of carries a faint sense of defiance that despite does not. Both are cuttable, and in most sentences both should be cut.
examples: In spite of the fact that the forecast called for snow, nobody salted the roads.
He kept the appointment in spite of the fact that he could barely stand up.
In spite of the fact that she had been passed over twice, she stayed another six years.
The exhibit opened on time in spite of the fact that half the crates arrived the night before.
In spite of the fact that everyone knew the answer, nobody said it out loud.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb by function — a prepositional phrase that takes a noun phrase and never a clause
entries.register: formal, legal — contract and statutory boilerplate, with no life at all outside drafted documents
entries.clause: none — a fronted adverbial that overrides other provisions of the same instrument
entries.pattern: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary [in this Agreement / herein / contained herein], [main clause]. · Notwithstanding anything in [Section X] to the contrary, [main clause]. · Notwithstanding anything to the contrary, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the whole phrase, always — the override has to close before the operative sentence begins. No commas inside it. It is not a conjunction and cannot join two clauses.
variants: notwithstanding anything herein to the contrary
notwithstanding anything contained herein to the contrary
notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement
notwithstanding the foregoing (narrower — it reaches only the text just above)
entries.meaning: The override switch of American contract drafting: whatever else the document says, this sentence wins. Drafters and courts both treat it warily, because an agreement with four of them scattered through it has no readable order of priority — style guides tell you to name the provision you mean to override instead. Its reach is the whole instrument, which is what separates it from notwithstanding the foregoing.
examples: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Agreement, Licensor's total liability shall not exceed the fees paid in the preceding twelve months.
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary herein, either party may seek injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction.
Notwithstanding anything in Section 8 to the contrary, the confidentiality obligations survive termination.
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary, no provision of this Article shall be construed to waive a Tenant's statutory rights.
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in the Plan, no award may be repriced without shareholder approval.

entries.type: subordinating; the same word is also a preposition that can stand either before its object (notwithstanding the delay) or after it (the delay notwithstanding), and a conjunctive adverb in its own right
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Notwithstanding that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] notwithstanding that [clause]. · Notwithstanding the fact that [clause], [main clause]. · Notwithstanding [noun phrase], [main clause]. (preposition) · [main clause], [noun phrase] notwithstanding. (postposed preposition)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it trails. As a preposition it takes no comma at all — notwithstanding the delay — and neither does the postposed form, the delay notwithstanding.
variants: notwithstanding the fact that
notwithstanding + noun phrase (preposition)
entries.meaning: "Although," in the register of contracts and court opinions. Its oddity is that the prepositional form can sit before its object or after it: notwithstanding any provision to the contrary and any provision to the contrary notwithstanding are both standard, and the postposed version is a legal signature.
examples: Notwithstanding that the lease had expired, the tenant remained in possession.
The board approved the transfer notwithstanding that two directors objected.
Notwithstanding that he had signed the waiver, the court allowed the claim.
Notwithstanding the fact that the deadline had passed, the agency accepted the filing.
The contract stands, the earlier memorandum notwithstanding.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal) — an anaphoric adverbial pointing back at the text just read
entries.register: formal, legal — contracts, bylaws, board resolutions, and statutes; in ordinary prose it reads as a parody of a lawyer
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial carving an exception out of the provision immediately above it
entries.pattern: Notwithstanding the foregoing, [main clause]. · Notwithstanding the foregoing [sentence/Section/subsection], [main clause]. · The foregoing notwithstanding, [main clause]. (postposed)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, and a period or a semicolon in front of it when what precedes is a complete sentence — it is an adverbial, not a conjunction, so a comma alone there is a comma splice.
variants: the foregoing notwithstanding (postposed)
notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding sentence
notwithstanding anything to the contrary (broader — it reaches the entire document)
entries.meaning: The drafting equivalent of "except for what I am about to say." It carves an exception out of the provision the reader has just finished, and its scope is exactly that — unlike notwithstanding anything to the contrary, it does not claim the whole agreement, though drafters argue endlessly about how far back "the foregoing" runs, which is why careful ones name the section instead.
examples: Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Company may terminate this Agreement immediately upon the Executive's conviction of a felony.
Subscriptions renew automatically. Notwithstanding the foregoing, a subscriber may cancel within thirty days of renewal for a full refund.
Notwithstanding the foregoing sentence, no notice is required in the event of an emergency repair.
The foregoing notwithstanding, the Board retains discretion to accelerate vesting.
Notwithstanding the foregoing, nothing in this Section limits either party's indemnification obligations.

entries.type: subordinating; bare regardless is a conjunctive adverb (Regardless, they went ahead) and regardless of is a preposition (regardless of the weather)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Regardless of the fact that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] regardless of the fact that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; usually no comma when it trails.
variants: irrespective of the fact that (more formal). Irregardless is nonstandard — avoid it.
entries.meaning: Concedes a known fact and dismisses it as beside the point. It runs a shade colder than despite the fact that: despite acknowledges the obstacle, while regardless refuses to weigh it at all. Cut it to although or even though unless that dismissiveness is exactly what you want heard.
examples: Regardless of the fact that the permit had been denied, construction continued.
They billed us for the full month regardless of the fact that we moved out on the ninth.
Regardless of the fact that she was the only qualified applicant, the search was reopened.
He repeated the claim regardless of the fact that it had been corrected twice on air.
Regardless of the fact that the ballot was printed wrong, the results were certified.
related: in spite of the fact that

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, usually verbless
entries.pattern: [main clause], albeit [adjective/adverb/noun phrase/prepositional phrase]. · [main clause], albeit [determiner] [adjective] [noun]. · [main clause], albeit [adverb], [rest of the sentence].
entries.punctuation: Always a comma before albeit, and commas on both sides when it interrupts. It is not a coordinator, so it cannot join two full independent clauses across a comma — if a subject and a tensed verb follow, use although.
entries.meaning: A fossil of all be it ("although it be"), and it still behaves like one: it takes a phrase rather than a full clause, and it concedes a qualification rather than a fact. He agreed, albeit reluctantly is right; He agreed, albeit he was reluctant is the classic overreach, and although is the fix.
examples: The meeting produced a decision, albeit a temporary one.
She agreed to testify, albeit under protest.
Sales recovered, albeit slowly, over the following two quarters.
It's a real solution, albeit an expensive one.
He offered an apology, albeit one that blamed everybody else.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal)
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial pointing back at a concession already made
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. All the same, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; all the same, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] all the same. · [Independent clause], all the same.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position. At the end of a sentence it takes a comma when it lands as an afterthought and none when it is fused to the verb phrase (she went all the same). Between two independent clauses it needs a period or a semicolon — a comma alone is a comma splice.
variants: just the same (identical in meaning, a shade more casual)
all the same to me/you (a different idiom altogether — indifference, not concession)
entries.meaning: "That changes nothing." It points backward at a concession the speaker has just granted and refuses to let it govern, which puts it next to nevertheless — the difference is tone, since all the same is what people say and nevertheless is what they write. Keep it apart from the frozen it's all the same to me, where the words mean no preference rather than no surrender.
examples: The reviews were brutal. All the same, the theater was packed every night.
He apologized, and I appreciated it; all the same, I'm not lending him the truck again.
She knew the trail was closed. She went all the same.
All the same, I'd feel better if somebody called ahead.
The rent was more than we wanted to pay. We took the place, just the same.
It's a long drive for one night; just the same, I'm glad we went.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb
entries.register: informal for anyhow; anyways is nonstandard — casual regional American speech, and a red flag in writing
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial dismissing what was just granted
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Anyhow, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; anyhow, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] anyhow.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and no comma before it in final position (we went anyhow). A period or a semicolon in front of it when it opens a new independent clause; a comma there is a comma splice.
variants: anyway (the standard form, with a fuller entry among the conjunctive adverbs)
anyways (nonstandard; common in casual speech across the South and Midwest, never in edited prose)
any how (not a word — always one word)
entries.meaning: The concessive job of the anyway family: the fact just granted is real, and the main clause happened regardless. Anyhow is fully standard and a touch more casual than anyway; anyways is the dialectal form carrying the old adverbial -s, which an American hears constantly and should write only in dialogue. All three also do discourse work — returning to a dropped thread, closing a phone call — and that sense belongs with anyway.
examples: The forecast said rain all day. We drove up anyhow.
Nobody asked my opinion; anyhow, here it is.
Anyhow, the point is that the deposit never cleared.
"It's probably too late to call." "Call him anyhow."
The store was closing in ten minutes, but they let us in anyhow.
He told her the lease forbade dogs. She got the dog anyways. (nonstandard — casual speech only)

entries.ipa: /ət ˈðæt/ — at reduces to /ət/ inside the phrase
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal, clause-final)
entries.register: informal to neutral; the concessive sense is dated and now mostly regional, while the additive sense is everywhere
entries.clause: none — a clause-final tag
entries.pattern: [Independent clause] at that. · [Independent clause], at that. · [noun phrase], and [adjective] one at that. (the additive sense)
entries.punctuation: It sits at the very end of its clause. A comma in front of it is normal when it arrives as an afterthought and optional when it is fused to what precedes. It is not a conjunction and can never join two clauses.
variants: at that in the additive sense ("and moreover": a long drive, and a boring one at that)
let it go at that, leave it at that (fixed idioms, not connectors)
entries.meaning: Two senses share the shape, and only the surrounding sentence sorts them out. The common one is additive — a used car, and an old one at that — which belongs with moreover. The concessive one, "in spite of all that, contrary to what you'd expect," is older and now much rarer: he might win at that means the speaker has just talked themselves out of their own objection. Americans meet that sense mostly in older fiction and in regional speech.
examples: He may be right at that. (concessive — "in spite of what I just said")
I laughed when he suggested walking, and then we walked, and it wasn't bad at that.
"Nobody will notice." "They might, at that."
The old wiring came through the storm at that, which is more than the new panel did.
It was a two-hour meeting, and a pointless one at that. (the common additive sense — "and moreover")
We agreed to leave it at that. (fixed idiom, not a connector)

entries.type: subordinating — a frozen subjunctive with inversion
entries.register: archaic and literary — hymns, proverbs, nineteenth-century prose, and one song lyric every American knows
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession, universal over degree — "no matter how"
entries.pattern: Be it ever so [adjective], [main clause]. · Be [subject] ever so [adjective], [main clause]. · Be [subject] ne'er so [adjective], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause, which is always fronted. It is a clause and not an adverbial, so the semicolon question never arises.
variants: be it never so (the older form)
be he ne'er so, be she ne'er so (the subject changes, and ne'er stands for never)
however + adjective, no matter how (the modern forms)
entries.meaning: The subjunctive be thrown to the front of its clause, exactly as in come what may, conceding every degree of the adjective at once: be it ever so humble means "no matter how humble it is." Modern English says however humble it is. What keeps the formula alive for Americans is the song — be it ever so humble, there's no place like home — and beyond that it belongs to Shakespeare, the King James Bible, and the hymnal.
examples: "Be it ever so humble, there's no place like home." (John Howard Payne, "Home, Sweet Home," 1823)
Be it ever so slight, an error in the survey has to be corrected before the deed is recorded.
Be he ne'er so poor, no man was turned away from that door.
Be she ne'er so fair, she has not a penny to her name.
"Be it never so true, it were not fit to be spoken here."
Be it ever so cold, the mill opened at six.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial, not a clause connector
