entries.pattern: [statement]. Be that as it may, [statement]. · [statement]; be that as it may, [statement].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it. Because it is an adverb and not a conjunction, it cannot join two independent clauses with a comma alone — put a period or a semicolon in front of it, exactly as you would with however or nevertheless.
entries.meaning: A frozen subjunctive meaning "granting all of that." It concedes everything the other side has just said and then sets the whole pile aside, which makes it a favorite of judges, editors, and people trying to end an argument. It always points backward, at something already stated.
examples: The costs are real. Be that as it may, the project is going forward.
He may well have been provoked; be that as it may, he threw the first punch.
"The forecast says clear skies." "Be that as it may, I'm bringing a jacket."
The data are three years old. Be that as it may, nothing since then contradicts them.
She never signed the form; be that as it may, everyone treated her as a member.

entries.ipa: /bɪˌliv ɪt ər ˈnɑt/ · casually /bəˌliv ɪɾ ər ˈnɑt/, with the t of it flapped
entries.type: subordinating — a frozen concessive-conditional clause, built exactly like like it or not
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition (frozen imperative plus alternative)
entries.pattern: Believe it or not, [main clause]. · [main clause], believe it or not. · [main clause] — believe it or not — [continuation]. · Whether you believe it or not, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Always set off by a comma, at the front, at the end, or on both sides when it interrupts. It is an adverbial, not a conjunction: Believe it or not, the check cleared, the bank called to confirm is a comma splice.
variants: whether you believe it or not (the full form, and blunter)
if you can believe it
believe you me (a different idiom — emphasis, not concession)
entries.meaning: A whether clause with the whether dropped and the verb left standing in the imperative, exactly like like it or not. It runs through both branches — you believe it, you don't — and reports that the main clause holds either way, which in practice makes it a flag on a surprising fact more than a real concession. Like it or not warns; believe it or not invites.
examples: Believe it or not, the permit came through in nine days.
He had never seen the ocean before that trip, believe it or not.
Believe it or not, that's the third time this month the main has broken.
The cheapest flight was the nonstop — believe it or not — and it left at a civilized hour.
Whether you believe it or not, I never got the invoice.
She reads every word of the terms of service, believe it or not.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition (frozen, with inversion)
entries.pattern: Come what may, [main clause]. · [main clause], come what may.
entries.punctuation: Always set off by a comma, at the front or at the end.
entries.meaning: "No matter what happens" — another frozen subjunctive, this one with the verb thrown to the front. It looks forward, where be that as it may looks back, and it reads as a vow rather than as an argument.
examples: Come what may, the wedding is happening on the fourteenth.
She promised to see the project through, come what may.
Come what may, this family has dinner together on Sundays.
He had made up his mind to enlist, come what may.
Come what may, the doors open at seven and the curtain goes up at eight.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial pointing back at a condition or a moment already named
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Even then, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; even then, [independent clause]. · [conditional clause], and even then [main clause]. · [Independent clause] even then.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position. Between two independent clauses it takes a period or a semicolon, never a bare comma. Riding behind and it needs no punctuation of its own: if the parts arrive Monday, and even then it's tight.
variants: even so (which points back at a granted fact rather than a hypothetical)
and even then (the commonest shape in speech)
even at that
entries.meaning: The adverb that finishes what even if starts: the if clause names the best case and even then says the main claim survives it. It is anaphoric — it has to point back at a condition or a time already on the table — and that is the split from even so, which points back at a fact. It also does plain temporal work (he was nine, and even then he could name every state capital), and only context sorts the two.
examples: We might get the permit by June. Even then, nothing gets poured before August.
You'd have to sell both cars, and even then you'd come up short.
The drug helps maybe a third of patients; even then, the effect is modest.
Assume every witness is telling the truth. Even then, the timeline doesn't work.
They may reopen the road tonight. Even then, I'd take the long way around.
He was nine when they moved here, and even then he could name every state capital. (temporal — "as early as that")

entries.type: conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: none — a supplementary adverbial, often a whole turn by itself
entries.pattern: Granted, [statement]. · [statement], granted, [continuation]. · [independent clause]; granted, [independent clause]. · [independent clause] — granted — [continuation]. · "Granted." (as a complete reply)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a sentence, commas on both sides when it interrupts. Because it is an adverb and not a conjunction, it cannot join two independent clauses with a comma alone: put a period or a semicolon in front of it, exactly as you would with however or nevertheless. It's expensive, granted, it's also the only one that fits is a comma splice; It's expensive; granted, it's also the only one that fits is not.
entries.meaning: Concedes the other person's point, usually so that the speaker can turn around and qualify it. In American conversation it is the standard one-word way of saying "fair enough, but." The subordinating granted that is the same word doing a heavier job.
examples: Granted, the first hour is slow, but the last twenty minutes are worth it.
"It's expensive." "Granted. It's also the only one that fits."
The house needs work, granted, though the lot alone is worth the price.
Granted, I've only driven it once, and I already want one.
She's the youngest person on the staff — granted — and she's also the only one who has shipped anything.
It's a long drive; granted, the last twenty miles make up for it.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (formerly also subordinating)
entries.clause: none in modern use — a sentence adverbial meaning "nevertheless"
entries.pattern: [statement]; howbeit, [statement]. · Howbeit [clause], [main clause]. (obsolete subordinating use)
entries.punctuation: As with any conjunctive adverb, a semicolon or a period in front of it and a comma after. The obsolete subordinating form takes a comma after its clause.
variants: howbe
howsobeit
entries.meaning: The dead ancestor of albeit, built the same way out of how be it. It survives in the King James Bible, in deliberate period pastiche, and in the occasional antique-sounding legal opinion; no living American register uses it. Read it as nevertheless.
examples: "Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect." (1 Corinthians 2:6, King James Version)
The general was warned; howbeit, he pressed the attack at dawn.
Howbeit the terms were harsh, the town accepted them.
She had every right to refuse; howbeit, she signed.
Howbeit, the matter was never spoken of again.

entries.ipa: /ˌlaɪk ɪt ər ˈnɑt/ · casually /ˌlaɪk ɪɾ ər ˈnɑt/, with the t of it flapped
entries.type: subordinating — a frozen concessive-conditional clause; the bare word like is also a preposition (a house like ours), a verb (I like it), a noun (likes and dislikes), an informal subordinator of manner (like I said), and an informal quotative (she was like, no)
entries.register: neutral to informal; the full whether you like it or not is blunter still
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition (frozen, imperative plus alternative)
entries.pattern: Like it or not, [main clause]. · [main clause], like it or not. · Like [noun phrase] or not, [main clause]. · Whether [subject] like(s) it or not, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Always set off by a comma, at the front or at the end. It is an adverbial, not a conjunction that joins clauses, so it cannot splice two independent clauses together: We're going, like it or not, the tickets are bought is a comma splice — put a period or a semicolon after not.
variants: whether you like it or not (the full form)
ready or not
want to or not
entries.meaning: The spoken cousin of whether or not: a whether clause with the whether dropped and the verb left standing in the imperative. It runs through both branches — you like it, you don't — and reports that the main clause holds either way. More often a warning than a concession, which is why it lands hardest at the front of a sentence, and why it so rarely appears in writing that is trying to be polite.
examples: Like it or not, the deadline moved up to the fifteenth.
We're all on the new system Monday, like it or not.
Like it or not, that stretch of highway is the only way in.
She's the deciding vote, like it or not.
Whether you like it or not, the two of you are going to have to share an office.
Ready or not, the doors open at nine.

entries.type: prepositional in form, concessive in force — it takes a noun phrase and never a clause
entries.register: archaic — Middle and Early Modern English; Chaucer, Spenser, Shakespeare, and Sir Walter Scott, and nothing written since
entries.clause: none — a concessive prepositional phrase
entries.pattern: Maugre [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] maugre [noun phrase]. · Maugre [possessive] [noun], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase and none when it trails — the rules that govern despite. It cannot join two clauses.
variants: mauger, malgre, maulgre (older spellings — the word was never settled)
in spite of, despite (the modern forms)
malgré (the living French word it came from)
entries.meaning: Old French maugré, "ill will": to do a thing maugre someone was to do it against their spite, which is where the modern phrase in spite of gets its noun. It dropped out of English in the seventeenth century and survives only in period text and deliberate antiquarian writing. An American meets it in Twelfth Night and in Scott's novels, and nowhere else.
examples: "I love thee so that, maugre all thy pride, / Nor wit nor reason can my passion hide." (Twelfth Night, III.i)
"Maugre thy strength, place, youth, and eminence, … thou art a traitor." (King Lear, V.iii)
The abbey held its lands maugre the bishop's decree.
Maugre every warning, the young laird rode north at first light.
He kept his seat at the table, maugre the whispering of the whole company.
Maugre wind and tide, the packet made harbor before dark.
related: in spite of the fact that

entries.type: conjunctive adverb by function — a frozen imperative used as a parenthetical connector
entries.register: informal, spoken; more British and Irish than American, but current in American conversation and in dialogue
entries.clause: none — a parenthetical adverbial hanging a qualification on what was just said
entries.pattern: [Statement], mind you, [continuation]. · [Statement] — mind you, [statement]. · Mind you, [statement]. · [Statement], mind you.
entries.punctuation: Always fenced with commas, dashes, or parentheses. Because it is an adverbial and not a conjunction, it cannot hold two independent clauses together: He paid, mind you, he took his time about it is a comma splice — write He paid — mind you, he took his time about it.
variants: mind, mind you now (older and more regional)
note that (the formal equivalent)
granted, to be fair (the American near-equivalents)
entries.meaning: Flags the next thing — or the thing just said — as a qualification the listener had better not overlook: "I'm granting this, so don't hold it against me later." It is the spoken hedge that keeps a compliment from being total or a complaint from being unfair. In American English it carries a faint British accent; granted and to be fair do the same work without one.
examples: He's the best hitter on the team. He can't field, mind you.
Mind you, I only heard this secondhand.
The place was spotless — mind you, they'd had a week's notice we were coming.
She never complained, mind you, but you could see what the shifts were costing her.
I'm not saying he's wrong. Mind you, I'm not saying he's right either.
It's a good price. Mind you, you'll spend it twice over on repairs.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb
entries.register: archaic and poetic — Spenser, Milton, Keats, and nineteenth-century verse; dead in every modern register
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial meaning "nevertheless"
entries.pattern: [Statement]; natheless, [statement]. · Natheless, [statement]. · [statement] natheless [continuation]. (bare inside a line of verse)
entries.punctuation: Modern editing gives it a semicolon or a period in front and a comma after, like any conjunctive adverb; the poets who used it often left it unpunctuated inside the line.
variants: nathless, natheles, nathelesse (the spelling was never fixed)
ne'ertheless
nevertheless (the surviving form)
entries.meaning: The ancestor of nevertheless, from Old English na þe læs, "not the less." It had fallen out of ordinary use by the seventeenth century and survived after that as a poetic archaism — Milton reached for it in Paradise Lost, and the Romantics reached for it because Milton had. An American meets it in a poetry anthology; in prose it reads as pastiche.
examples: "Nathless he so endur'd, till on the beach / Of that inflamed sea he stood." (Milton, Paradise Lost, I)
The road was washed out; natheless the mail came through.
Natheless, the lady kept her counsel and said nothing to the court.
He was warned of the ford; natheless he rode into it.
Natheless she loved him, and would not hear a word said against him.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal) — a concessive disjunct
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial conceding a point before the objection arrives
entries.pattern: No doubt [independent clause], but [independent clause]. · [subject] no doubt [verb phrase], but [independent clause]. · [independent clause], no doubt. · Doubtless [independent clause], but [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: A fronted no doubt needs no comma after it — it leans on the clause it opens — though one is fine when the phrase is meant to stand apart. Comma before it at the end of a sentence. It is not a conjunction, so keep the but when you are joining two clauses.
variants: doubtless (compressed, and more literary)
doubtlessly (widely disliked — write doubtless)
undoubtedly (emphatic rather than concessive: it agrees instead of conceding)
no doubt about it (a fixed emphatic tag)
entries.meaning: Concedes something in advance, and the concession is usually thin: no doubt she meant well has a but waiting behind it almost every time, which makes the phrase a polite way of not really conceding at all. That ironic edge is the whole difference from undoubtedly, where the speaker actually agrees. Doubtless does the same job a register higher.
examples: No doubt the intentions were good, but the rollout was a disaster.
She'll have a reason, no doubt.
No doubt you've heard a different version of this story.
Doubtless the committee has its reasons; it has not shared them with the faculty.
The contractor was no doubt busy, which does not explain three unreturned calls.
Doubtless he meant it kindly, and it landed badly all the same.

entries.type: subordinating — a frozen stacked negative
entries.register: archaic and formal for not but that; not but what is dialectal and nonstandard — regional American and British speech, never edited prose
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (parenthetical disclaimer)
entries.pattern: [statement], not but that [clause]. · [statement]. Not but that [clause]. · [statement], not but what [clause]. (nonstandard)
entries.punctuation: A comma, a dash, or a period in front of it — it always arrives as an afterthought. Never run it onto the previous clause with no punctuation at all.
variants: not but what (dialectal)
not but (the bare older form)
not that (the living modern form)
entries.meaning: The eighteenth- and nineteenth-century ancestor of not that: a stacked negative meaning "it is not that … not," which comes out as "though of course." She never spoke of the money, not but that she needed it says she needed it badly. Americans meet it in Austen, Dickens, and Trollope; not but what is the same phrase in country speech, and modern writing has handed the whole job to not that.
examples: She never spoke of the money, not but that she needed it.
He declined the invitation — not but that he was flattered to be asked.
I have no quarrel with the arrangement, not but that I should have preferred to be consulted.
"He's a decent enough landlord, not but what the roof's wanted fixing these ten years." (dialectal)
The family said nothing at the time, not but that the whole village knew.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal) in the concessive sense; the older sense inverts the clause behind it
entries.register: informal and regional — the concessive opener is a New York, New Jersey, and Boston signature, familiar nationally from movies and television
entries.clause: none — a discourse-initial adverbial prefacing an objection
entries.pattern: Not for nothing, but [independent clause]. · Not for nothing, [independent clause]. · Not for nothing [auxiliary] [subject] [verb phrase]. (the older inverted sense)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, and the but that usually follows keeps its ordinary place. It cannot join two independent clauses on its own.
variants: no offense, but, with all due respect (the same softener without the regional accent)
not for nothing did + subject (the older "for good reason" sense)
not for nothing is it called …
entries.meaning: Two senses that pull in opposite directions. The older one means "for good reason" and inverts the clause after it: not for nothing is that stretch called the worst merge in the state. The newer one — the one an American actually hears — is a Northeastern discourse opener that softens an objection just before it lands, exactly like no offense, but: it announces that the speaker knows the next sentence may sting.
examples: Not for nothing, but the last two times we tried this, the server went down.
Not for nothing, but you're the one who picked the restaurant.
"Not for nothing, Counselor, your client's story has changed twice."
Not for nothing, I've been doing this twenty years and I've never seen a rider like that.
Not for nothing is that stretch of I-95 called the worst merge in the state. (the older sense — "for good reason")
Not for nothing did the neighbors start calling the block "the canyon." (older sense, inverted)

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (parenthetical disclaimer)
entries.pattern: [statement]. Not that [clause]. · Not that [clause], but [main clause]. · [statement] — not that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Set it off with a period, a dash, or parentheses; when but follows, a comma goes between the two halves. Never attach it to the previous sentence with a comma alone.
entries.meaning: Heads off an inference the speaker expects the listener to draw, and denies it — usually with a wink, since not that it matters concedes that it does matter, or the sentence would not exist. It is one of the most common concessive moves in American speech and almost never appears in formal writing.
examples: He's moving to Denver. Not that he told any of us.
Not that I'm counting, but this is the fourth time she has rescheduled.
The place has no sign and no website — not that they need one.
I'd have picked a different color. Not that anybody asked.
Not that it's my business, but the contractor's truck hasn't moved in a week.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal)
entries.register: informal and regional — colloquial American speech with a rural, older-generation flavor; not standard written English
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial dismissing what was just granted
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Still and all, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; still and all, [independent clause]. · Still and all, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it. Between two independent clauses it needs a period or a semicolon in front — a comma alone is a comma splice, exactly as with however.
variants: still (the standard one-word form)
all the same, just the same
when all's said and done
entries.meaning: A colloquial doubling of still, where and all adds nothing but breath and warmth. It grants everything just said and then holds the line anyway. It is a spoken form — an American hears it from an older relative or reads it in dialogue — and an editor cuts it to still or all the same in anything formal.
examples: The truck has two hundred thousand miles on it. Still and all, it starts every morning.
She was rude about it; still and all, she wasn't wrong.
Still and all, somebody should have called the family first.
We knew the odds. Still and all, it stung to lose that way.
The place is falling apart. Still and all, I'd rather be there than anywhere else.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal) — a concessive disjunct
entries.register: formal to neutral — a writer's phrase; in speech it sounds bookish
entries.clause: none — a sentence adverbial conceding a point, almost always ahead of a but
entries.pattern: [Independent clause], to be sure, but [independent clause]. · To be sure, [independent clause]. But [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], to be sure.
entries.punctuation: Commas around it wherever it sits. It is an adverbial and not a conjunction, so the but that so often follows still has to be there — drop it and two independent clauses are left spliced.
variants: admittedly, granted (the same move, one conversational and one neutral)
it is true that
sure (the informal one-word version: sure, it's expensive, but …)
entries.meaning: The essayist's concession: it grants the strongest point on the other side in order to show that the argument survives it. It nearly always has a but or a yet behind it — a to be sure with no reversal after it has left its sentence unfinished. Against granted, which is conversational, this is the written form, and it carries a faint whiff of the nineteenth-century critic.
examples: The evidence is thin, to be sure, but every piece of it points the same way.
To be sure, the first two seasons are uneven. The third is one of the best things ever put on television.
He was not the most experienced candidate, to be sure; he was plainly the most prepared.
To be sure, nobody expected the program to pay for itself in a single year.
The translation loses the puns, to be sure, and it keeps the argument perfectly intact.

entries.type: subordinating — a rhetorical question standing in for a concessive clause
entries.register: archaic and poetic — Shakespeare, Milton, the hymnal, and nineteenth-century verse; dead in modern prose
entries.clause: interrogative in form, concessive in force — "what does it matter that …"
entries.pattern: What though [clause]? [main clause]. · What though [clause], [main clause]. · What though [noun phrase]? [main clause].
entries.punctuation: A question mark after the what though clause when it is put as a question, a comma when it runs straight into the main clause. Both are standard in older text, and modern editions differ on which to print.
variants: though, even though (the modern forms)
what if (the surviving relative — it asks rather than concedes)
what matter though
entries.meaning: A rhetorical question doing a concessive clause's work: what though the field be lost? means "granted the field is lost — it changes nothing." The subjunctive verb (be, were) is part of the formula. Milton gave it its most famous outing and the hymn writers kept it alive through the nineteenth century; an American now meets it in poetry and in older hymns, nowhere else.
examples: "What though the field be lost? / All is not lost." (Milton, Paradise Lost, I)
"What though the spicy breezes / Blow soft o'er Ceylon's isle." (Reginald Heber, "From Greenland's Icy Mountains," 1819)
What though the night be long? The watch is set and the gate is barred.
What though he had neither name nor fortune, the girl would have him.
"What though our lot be hard, we are not therefore without hope."
